q: According to the book, what is the core weakness of HHH alignment under agentic conditions?
options: Its values are wrong for agents
It applies only to open-source models
It names desirable values but not how to resolve conflicts among them
explanation: Agents hit value conflicts more often and with bigger consequences, so they need priority orders, not just a list of values. (Barron, The Claw AI Agent Ecosystem, §10.1)

q: An agent reviewing a user's code softens its criticism so much the review becomes inaccurate. Which conflict is this?
explanation: Protecting the user's confidence (harmlessness) wins over an accurate evaluation (honesty), the chronic tension in feedback tasks. (Barron, The Claw AI Agent Ecosystem, §10.1)

q: In the example value priority list, which item resolves the conflict over what "archive old emails" should cover?
options: Right to understand what the agent will do
explanation: Confirming scope before acting settles the helpfulness vs. harmlessness tension in that example. (Barron, The Claw AI Agent Ecosystem, §10.1)

q: SOUL.md says to always confirm before sending email, but the AGENTS.md email tool sets requireConfirmation to false. What does the book say usually happens?
options: SOUL.md wins because it is loaded first
The more specific AGENTS.md setting wins and silently overrides SOUL.md
The model asks the operator which file to follow
explanation: This is the common incoherence failure. Pre-deployment review should check every SOUL.md gate has a matching AGENTS.md rule. (Barron, The Claw AI Agent Ecosystem, §10.2)

q: Which identity file does the book describe as relationship policy?
explanation: USER.md calibrates how the agent works with one particular person. (Barron, The Claw AI Agent Ecosystem, §10.2)

q: In the six-step elicitation method, what happens in step 2?
options: Generate 3 to 5 ambiguous instructions for each tool
explanation: Step 2 builds an edge case battery of instructions a reasonable person could read in two different ways. (Barron, The Claw AI Agent Ecosystem, §10.3)

q: In the book's table of operation classes, which has the lowest ambiguity?
explanation: Creation is usually clear from context. Cleaning and deleting rank highest because scope and undo path are both unclear. (Barron, The Claw AI Agent Ecosystem, §10.3)

q: After one unusual session, MEMORY.md records that the user dislikes detailed answers, and the agent stays brief for weeks. Which loop amplified the error?
options: Loop 3: memory growth and context cost (balancing)
None; this is a model defect
explanation: Whatever is recorded in memory shapes later sessions, so a wrong entry keeps reinforcing itself until corrected. (Barron, The Claw AI Agent Ecosystem, §10.4)

q: In the book's application of Meadows' leverage points to a Claw deployment, which is rated highest leverage?
explanation: How the operator frames the agent drives every downstream choice, though it is also the hardest to change. (Barron, The Claw AI Agent Ecosystem, §10.4)

q: An operator leaves the SOUL.md hard boundaries section empty. How does the book characterize this?
options: A neutral default that defers to the operator
A safe choice since models are trained to avoid harm
A policy choice meaning the agent has no explicit harm floor
Acceptable as long as AGENTS.md is long
explanation: Without stated boundaries the agent relies only on generic training constraints not tuned to the deployment. (Barron, The Claw AI Agent Ecosystem, §10.5)
